title: SNAP restrictions on sweetened beverages and candy reduced restricted spending, calories, and sugar
source_unit: US SNAP purchases of sweetened beverages and candy, restricted spending, calories, sugar, substitution, shelf prices, taxes, retailer SNAP intensity, online purchases, and modeled welfare
geography: United States; first statewide SNAP restrictions on sweetened beverages and candy

observations.period: Working paper issued September 2026; first statewide SNAP restrictions

denominator.unit: SNAP purchase and retailer observations across implementing states and comparison settings; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

restricted_spending.unit: percent change in spending on restricted sweetened beverages and candy

fruit_drink_substitution.unit: eligible fruit drinks partly offset soda declines

snack_substitution.unit: candy restrictions reduce purchases of eligible snacks

tax_inclusive_price.unit: percent increase from losing SNAP sales-tax exemption

online_response.unit: spending declines remain large online, where checkout stigma is less salient

modeled_welfare.unit: US dollars per year in modeled welfare gains under nationwide adoption

observations.method: The paper studies the first statewide SNAP restrictions on sweetened beverages and candy using purchase, retailer, price, tax, and online-shopping comparisons, with substitution and modeled welfare analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose sample counts, confidence intervals, exact restriction definitions, follow-up length, or the full welfare model. Purchase changes are not the same as consumption, health, food security, or household welfare; the nationwide $1.1 billion estimate is modeled, not observed.
observations.subgroup: SNAP recipients and retailers with different SNAP intensity, including online purchases and categories affected by soda, candy, fruit-drink, and snack substitution.
observations.counterinterpretation: Households may substitute across products, stores, cash purchases, or time; lower purchases can reflect avoidance, stigma, or price/tax changes rather than healthier diets, and restriction burden may vary by disability, place, retailer access, and household preference.

related_sources.claim: P-EBT disbursement increased sugary-item spending by 16% among SNAP-eligible households with school-aged children.
SNAP sugary-drink restrictions change purchases while increasing perceived stigma and producing substitution toward still-eligible drinks.
USDA household food-security measures provide a welfare and access boundary that purchase data alone cannot establish.

boundary: This record adds a restriction-response and purchase-substitution layer to the US safety-net program. It does not establish long-run consumption, nutrition, health, food security, household welfare, or that modeled nationwide benefits outweigh unequal burden for every recipient.
